Chapter 5: Embracing Shortcuts and Convenience Without Guilt
There’s a quiet revolution happening in kitchens all around us. People are finally realizing—hey, convenience doesn’t have to be something you’re ashamed of. If you’re someone who dreads cooking, shortcuts aren’t just nice to have, they’re what make it possible to get food on the table.
Think about it: the world is packed with products designed to make life easier. But for some reason, a lot of us feel guilty about reaching for them, like real cooking only counts if you’re sweating over the stove for hours.
Picture a new parent, completely overwhelmed, just trying to survive those first months with a baby. At first, she feels like she’s failing because she’s using pre-chopped veggies, rotisserie chicken, and microwaveable grains. Shouldn’t she be making everything from scratch? But after a few days, she realizes—these shortcuts are the only way dinner actually happens. The guilt starts to melt away, replaced by a huge sense of relief.
And here’s something you might not expect—even seasoned cooks rely on shortcuts. Frozen veggies, jarred sauces, canned beans, pre-cooked proteins... these aren’t signs of laziness. They’re just smart tools that keep dinner doable when you’re busy, tired, or just not feeling it.
Let’s take another example—a young man working long hours. He comes home exhausted and, honestly, the idea of cooking from scratch is just too much. So, he keeps frozen meals handy, along with a few basics. On nights when he’s got a bit more energy, maybe he tosses in some fresh veggies or fries an egg to go on top. Suddenly, a frozen dinner feels more like a real meal. Over time, he gets creative—mixing and matching convenience foods to whip up something satisfying, fast, and affordable.
Here’s the trick: use those shortcuts strategically. Pre-washed greens, pre-cooked grains, rotisserie chicken—these can be the starting point for salads, grain bowls, even sandwiches. Jarred sauces can turn plain pasta or rice into something special. Canned beans? They’re perfect for soups, stews, or tossing into a salad for a protein boost.
And you know what else? It’s okay if every meal isn’t perfectly balanced or “healthy.” Sometimes, the best dinner is just a sandwich, or even a bowl of cereal. The real goal is to make cooking feel doable—not to chase some impossible ideal.
Little by little, these shortcuts become second nature. The kitchen starts to feel less like a battleground and more like a place to just nourish yourself. Cooking stops being a performance and becomes, well, practical. Guilt gives way to self-compassion.
Most people find that, once they embrace the right shortcuts, cooking’s no longer a burden. It’s just another part of life—something you can manage, even on your worst days. The focus shifts from doing things “the right way” to simply doing what works for you.
At the end of the day, there’s really only one rule that matters: if it gets food on the table, it counts.
